# Source audit notes

This page records what the Neon Pairs source-inspection tests check, how they discover files and where their evidence stops.

The audits run as Vitest tests under `scripts`. They inspect authored text and configuration rather than executing the application. Their value is fast, concrete feedback about a deliberately small codebase. Their regular expressions are visible and limited; a passing audit is evidence about those patterns, not a complete semantic proof of the architecture.

## File discovery

`scripts/source-files.ts` exports `sourceFiles(folder)`. It recursively calls `readdir` with directory entries, descends into directories and reads ordinary files as UTF-8. A link or special entry causes `Source contains a link or special file.` rather than being followed or ignored.

The helper returns path/text pairs. It does not apply `.gitignore`, infer TypeScript projects or skip directories based on a general exclusion list. Each test chooses a starting folder and filters the returned paths. This makes the scan boundary part of the test source.

The broad authored-TypeScript checks scan `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`, then retain paths matching `.ts` or `.tsx`. The shipped-source check scans `src` and omits files whose names contain `.test.` or `.fixture.`. CSS and HTML can participate in that latter source-text scan even though the TypeScript-only checks exclude them.

## Packages and compiler projects

The first test in `source-audit.test.ts` parses `package.json` as unknown data and reads `scripts/package.fixture.json` as the reviewed expected versions. It narrows object shapes before using their fields. It asserts that the runtime dependency names are exactly React and React DOM, then compares expected package versions against the combined manifest maps.

It reads `package-lock.json`, finds the root package entry and compares that entry's dependency and development-dependency maps against the manifest. This catches disagreement at the root. It does not independently audit every transitive package or establish what code an installed package executes.

The same test checks `type: module`, the five explicitly enumerated strictness settings in `tsconfig.base.json`, the existence of the app/Node/end-to-end config files, the exact typecheck script and the `vitest run` unit command. It does not compare every compiler option against a fixture. [TypeScript settings](typescript-settings.md) records the full current configuration.

## File length and type escapes

The authored-TypeScript test removes trailing whitespace at the end of the text, splits on line endings and checks for at most 200 lines. The technology specification's 100-line aim is not the threshold in this assertion. A file at 180 lines can satisfy the test while still deserving a behavior-based split during review.

The test rejects diagnostic suppression markers for ignore, nocheck and expected-error forms. A second expression rejects the standalone token `any`, selected `as` assertions, dynamic import and require calls. These are text patterns, so comments and strings can trigger them too.

The assertion pattern catches an `as` followed by an uppercase name, an opening brace or selected primitive/unknown forms. It does not reject every possible TypeScript assertion syntax. In particular, the source uses `as const` for named value objects and literal arrays. Calling this a complete cast prohibition would misdescribe the implemented check.

The static-import patterns search for `import` or `require` followed by an opening parenthesis, allowing whitespace. The compiler remains responsible for actual syntax and symbol resolution. A text scan is useful for the repository convention precisely because its behavior is simple to inspect, but it is not a parser.

## Core-effect scan

The pure-core filename set is `deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts`. For non-test, non-fixture source with one of those basenames, the audit rejects listed browser/global markers and a Math random call marker.

The matching is by basename extracted from either path separator, not by a fully resolved module identity. A new file with one of those names elsewhere under `src` would also be selected. Conversely, a new differently named core helper is not automatically added to this set just because a pure module imports it.

This is an important coverage limit. The check does not traverse imports and propagate a purity classification. It also does not cover every current data-only helper, such as `saved-format.ts`, through that set. Review still considers the operations and dependencies of changed modules. [Purity guide](purity-guide.md) explains that architectural reasoning.

## Shipped-source scan

For all selected non-test, non-fixture files under `src`, the audit rejects known audio, canvas and network constructs and a pattern for a deck diagnostic property on window. It also rejects the text markers `fixture`, `face-sheet` and `test-results` in shipped source.

The exact constructs include AudioContext, `new Audio`, audio/canvas markup, a fetch call marker and XMLHttpRequest. This is narrower than proving that every conceivable request mechanism or diagnostic exposure is absent. It does not inspect minified output produced by third-party tools.

The generated-output complement is `tests/build-output.e2e.test.ts`, which reads the built HTML and checks the unwanted fetch and preload markers. The browser complement opens the artifact. These checks have separate inputs and failure meanings; [Offline delivery](offline-delivery.md) connects them.

## Export and ownership conventions

`source-conventions.test.ts` builds its own TypeScript file list over the same four authored folders. Its export regex recognizes line-start declarations of exported constants, functions, interfaces, type aliases and classes, with an optional async marker for functions. It does not attempt to enumerate all legal ESM export syntax.

Its named-import regex collects names inside braces, strips an inline type marker and removes local aliases. The test creates a set of imported names, then asserts that every recognized export name is present in that set. For recognized exported constants it also records a single owner by name.

This is a repository-wide name check. It does not prove that a specific import resolves to the specific export being checked. A same-named import can satisfy the set membership, and re-export syntax or a different declaration form can escape recognition. Those limitations explain why direct imports remain useful to a human reader.

The practical intention is legibility: avoid publishing helpers that no actual behavior uses and avoid ambiguous ownership of exported values. The implementation enforces a recognizable subset of that intention, rather than a full reference graph.

## Predicate names and test names

Another expression recognizes exported function signatures with an explicit boolean or type-predicate return. It checks that the name begins with `is` or `has` followed by an uppercase letter. `isValidSize`, `isWon`, `isJsonObject` and `hasExactKeys` fit this style.

Because the pattern is textual, inferred return types and more elaborate signatures can fall outside it. This is a naming check for recognized yes-or-no exports, not a general attempt to infer every function's meaning.

Test names are inspected in files ending `.test.ts`. The pattern extracts recognized `test` titles and rejects requirement-ID forms such as an uppercase letter followed by two digits. Assertions may still carry requirement references; the check is about human-readable titles. Template-literal titles are included in the recognized forms.

## Environment reads

The environment-read test collects `process.env` access using a simple dotted or bracketed identifier pattern. It compares normalized path/name pairs against a fixed list. The expected pairs are:

| File | Name recorded by the expression |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/replay-cli.ts` | `INIT_CWD` |
| `scripts/replay.test.ts` | `npm_execpath` |
| `tests/browser-test.ts` | `EXECUTABLE_ENV` |
| `tests/browser-test.ts` | `NAMED_COMBINATION_ENV` |
| `tests/browser-test.ts` | `NPM_AGENT_ENV` |
| `tests/browser-test.ts` | `TEMP` and `TMP` |

For bracketed reads it records the variable identifier, not the string value held by that variable. The browser helper's constants correspond to executable selection, named-combination enforcement and npm's user-agent value. The test normalizes Windows separators before comparing the sorted unique set.

The expression does not model destructuring, aliases, computed string expressions or every possible environment access. It is a narrow check of the current authored forms. The fixed comparison makes accidental environment-dependent game behavior conspicuous within those forms.

## Interpreting a failure

A file-length failure names the file. An export failure names the unconsumed symbol or duplicate owner. A predicate failure names the function. The environment test gives a changed set of path/name pairs. These failures are most useful when read alongside the small regex that produced them.

A false positive in a comment is still a real failure of the textual test, but it does not demonstrate that the comment executes an effect. A false negative is also possible when syntax falls outside a pattern. Neither case justifies describing the audit as more powerful than it is.

Compiler checks, focused unit tests and browser journeys remain separate evidence. The source audits can establish that the manifest and root lock maps agree while a browser journey still fails, or that game transitions are correct while an authored file violates a convention. [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) treats those as distinct findings rather than flattening them into one pass/fail label.

# CSS organization

This page maps the Neon Pairs stylesheets to their components and explains the global cascade, layout formulas and visual-test seams.

Styles sit beside the behavior they present and are imported by components. They remain ordinary global CSS. File adjacency makes ownership discoverable, while selector choice and the cascade determine actual reach. There is no CSS module transformation, CSS-in-JS runtime or component-library theme layer in this source.

## Stylesheet ownership

| Stylesheet | Importing component or entry | Main responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/game/game.css` | `Game.tsx`; face-sheet entry also imports it | Root theme, page geometry, typography, focus outline and result space |
| `board/board.css` | `Board.tsx` | Viewport scrolling and grid dimensions |
| `board/card.css` | `Card.tsx` | Card states, back, face sizing and matched mark |
| `controls/control.css` | Deal and reproduction components | Shared native-control surface |
| `controls/controls.css` | `Controls.tsx` | Size selector and deal-button arrangement |
| `controls/reproduction.css` | Reproduction components | Disclosure, forms, textarea and load notice |
| `status/status.css` | `GameStatus.tsx` | Statistics and completion presentation |
| `art/face-sheet.css` | Face-sheet entry | Diagnostic placement of real cards |

A component import brings its styles into the application graph, and the build embeds the resulting CSS in the finished HTML. The source HTML has no separate stylesheet link to distribute. [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md) describes that assembly.

## Global foundation

`game.css` sets `system-ui, sans-serif`, a 16px root font size, 24px line height, light text on a dark background and `color-scheme: dark`. It defines the shared variables `--text`, `--secondary`, `--panel`, `--back`, `--face`, `--border` and `--green`.

The current values are `#f4f6ff` for text, `#b8bdd2` for secondary text, `#141827` for panels, `#1b2034` for card backs, `#111625` for face surfaces, `#757c9a` for borders and `#8bea7d` for matched green. The page background is `#090b14`.

The root also defines `--content-max: 1120px` and `--page-padding: 16px`. A global border-box reset applies to every element, body margin is zero and main uses full width up to that maximum with centered margins and page padding. These foundational rules affect diagnostics that deliberately import `game.css` as well as the main game.

Headings, paragraphs and help text have a small set of explicit margins and font sizes. Secondary text is generally 14px. The global `:focus-visible` outline is 3px white with a 2px offset. Because it is global, its interaction with scroll-container padding matters for cards as well as ordinary controls.

## The board owns its geometry

`board.css` defines board-specific custom properties on `.board-viewport`: card minimum 44px, card maximum 88px, gap 6px, padding 6px and border 1px. The viewport uses `overflow: auto`, contained overscroll, a rounded panel and `max-height: min(70dvh, 768px)`.

The viewport has `width: fit-content` and `max-width: 100%`. The inner board is a grid with a number of columns supplied by `--grid-size`, set from the current game size by `Board.tsx`. Track widths range from the card minimum to maximum.

Its width uses a clamp with these conceptual bounds:

```text
minimum = size * card-min + (size - 1) * gap
preferred = 100% of the available content width
maximum = size * card-max + (size - 1) * gap
```

For size 16, the inner minimum is 794px and maximum is 1498px. The viewport's own padding, border and any scrollbar are separate geometry. A narrow screen can therefore scroll the board rather than shrinking every track without limit or making the whole page wider than the viewport.

The width formula uses the scroll area's content box, which already accounts for occupied scrollbar space. `scrollbars.e2e.test.ts` runs with visible scrollbars at several viewport/size combinations to catch a layout that only works when Chromium hides them.

## Card states come from data

`Card.tsx` supplies `card` plus a state class returned by `describeCard`. `.card` is a square grid-placed native button with full available width, zero padding, a 2px border and an 8px radius. It uses the back surface until revealed or matched, when the face surface applies.

Hover changes the border to the text color. The matched selector appears after the hover selector and gives matched cards the green border. This ordering matters when a matched card remains hovered: its matched treatment continues to win. The class is derived from game data, not a CSS pseudo-state pretending to own the match.

The concealed back is a small rotated bordered span. Visible faces are SVG elements sized to the card. The matched check is a separate absolutely positioned SVG in the top-right corner with width and height at 16% of the card. The source comment explains that a mark much wider than roughly 17% would reach the face's top-right marker.

The card has `scroll-margin: 6px`, which works with nearest scrolling and the global focus outline. Its touch-action and user-selection properties support native pointer behavior. These rules are adjacent to the card because the face sheet also renders the same component outside the normal board layout.

## CSS and SVG share one surface value

The face renderer uses a viewBox of 0 0 100 100. Its main geometry takes the design color, with either a solid fill or outline stroke. A marker circle uses the same color, and its surround stroke is `var(--face)`.

That variable ties SVG geometry to the card's face background. Replacing the card surface without considering the marker surround could make the marker appear to have a mismatched halo. This is a direct dependency between the stylesheet and the inline SVG, even though face identity remains a data mapping in `face-design.ts`.

The matched mark is decorative and uses currentColor from CSS. It is separate from the identity marker, so its size and placement are checked for overlap at the smallest rendered card. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) cover identity design rather than stylesheet placement.

## Shared controls are deliberately narrow

`control.css` defines `.control`: minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px, a 1px border, 8px radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. Only button and select controls receive the pointer cursor rule. Inputs and textareas have `min-width: 0` so they can shrink within flex/grid layouts.

This class is applied explicitly to the game's form controls. The card component uses its own class and styling. A broad rule for every button would accidentally affect card rendering and diagnostic comparisons, which is why the current selectors distinguish those surfaces.

`controls.css` uses wrapping flex layout with a 12px gap and 16px bottom margin. The size control aligns label and select with a 12px gap. At widths up to 599px, the size row takes full width with spaced ends, while the direct deal buttons share available space.

These rules handle arrangement without replacing native select and button behavior. The CSS does not define a synthetic menu implementation or a separate touch activation model.

## Reproduction layout

The disclosure panel has 24px top margin, panel background, a 1px border and 12px radius. Its summary has a 44px minimum height and 12px by 16px padding. The open body is a grid with 12px gaps and its own inner padding.

The board-code form is a small grid; `.control-row` is a wrapping flex row with a 12px gap. The code input has a 16ch preferred width and flexible growth. The textarea fills its width and can resize vertically. On narrow screens the row buttons share space.

The load-status row sits outside the details element. It reserves at least 56px, wraps its children and gives the notice paragraph flexible width with `min-width: 0`. The conditional Resume button can therefore remain available even when the disclosure is closed. That structure is defined in JSX; the CSS provides room for the state it renders.

The separate `.game-result` area also reserves 56px and vertically centers its content. These reserved areas reduce layout movement when feedback changes. They do not add game-state transitions or determine which message is shown.

## Statistics and completion

`status.css` lays out the definition list with wrapping flex, a 12px row gap and a 24px column gap. Each statistic group has an 8ch minimum width. `dt` and `dd` are inline; labels use secondary text, and values use tabular numerals with reset margins.

Those `dt` and `dd` selectors are global, not scoped under `.stats`. That is harmless for the current single statistic list but is relevant when reading the cascade. File adjacency should not be mistaken for selector encapsulation.

The completion paragraph has padding, border, radius and bottom margin. The `celebrate` class applies a 600ms one-iteration pulse, whose midpoint changes background and opacity. Victory is still a game-derived paragraph after the pulse. A completed import renders the paragraph without that class because the session's celebration flag is false.

## Existing motion rules

The card transitions only border color for 120ms. A reduced-motion query removes that transition. The status sheet has a reduced-motion query that removes the completion animation. These are two local rules beside the elements they affect.

`motion.e2e.test.ts` reads computed transition properties and animation duration/iteration count, then runs with reduced motion and verifies the removals. This checks the browser result of the cascade rather than merely finding a media query in source. The broader motion rationale belongs to [Motion policy](../visuals/motion-policy.md).

## Visual evidence and diagnostic independence

`style.e2e.test.ts` measures root colors, typography, page padding, content maximum, board gap and card geometry. It also compares all computed styles before and after hover to ensure the observed change stays within border colors and checks that hovering does not alter exported progress.

`spacing.e2e.test.ts` inspects margins, padding and gaps in completed and paused-import states at phone and desktop widths. It excludes native option internals. The source's spacing values therefore have runtime evidence across more than the initial closed-panel view.

`art.e2e.test.ts` compares computed styles for a revealed game card and a face-sheet card after excluding placement-dependent properties. This checks that the card does not secretly rely on control styles loaded only by the game. It also measures actual geometry at the diagnostic card size.

For a CSS regression, the relevant chain is selector, inherited variable, rendered state and containing geometry. [Large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md), [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [Visual review checklist](../visuals/visual-review-checklist.md) cover the user-facing outcomes that this organization supports.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) for the exact validation and React effect. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md).

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. [Offline delivery](../architecture/offline-delivery.md) describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) and [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.

## Reading this group of pages

The existing preference representation is older than the feature-level storage conventions described in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). The existing writer continues to emit the preference aggregate. Likewise, [Retention policy](retention-policy.md) concerns saved lists; the current best-score map is an aggregate, not an attempt list.

For failures, begin with the operation that failed. Accessing `window.localStorage`, reading a key, parsing its string and writing a replacement are distinct stages. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers unavailable storage and the feature behavior built around it. [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) covers values that can be read but cannot be accepted. Both cases lead to usable in-memory state, but their evidence and timing differ.

[Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) maps the unit and browser evidence to the boundary being investigated. It also explains how a served origin, isolated context and operation-specific store double make a persistence report reproducible.
# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.

The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.

## Retained locally does not mean backed up

The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.

# Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. # Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.

The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.

## Retained locally does not mean backed up

The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.
# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) for the exact validation and React effect. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md).

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. [Offline delivery](../architecture/offline-delivery.md) describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) and [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.

## Reading this group of pages

The existing preference representation is older than the feature-level storage conventions described in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). The existing writer continues to emit the preference aggregate. Likewise, [Retention policy](retention-policy.md) concerns saved lists; the current best-score map is an aggregate, not an attempt list.

For failures, begin with the operation that failed. Accessing `window.localStorage`, reading a key, parsing its string and writing a replacement are distinct stages. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers unavailable storage and the feature behavior built around it. [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) covers values that can be read but cannot be accepted. Both cases lead to usable in-memory state, but their evidence and timing differ.

[Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) maps the unit and browser evidence to the boundary being investigated. It also explains how a served origin, isolated context and operation-specific store double make a persistence report reproducible.

# Competition results and local records

This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs.

The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.

## The competition boundary

A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.

For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.

The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time.

## What the game saves today

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.

An example stored value is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 10,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 24
  }
}
```

There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.

The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.

[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.

## Diagnostic entries and configured outputs

`art/index.html` and `art/face-sheet.tsx` form a separate face-sheet build with `art/face-sheet.css`. It imports the real card and design definitions to render every face at a controlled size. `vite.art.config.ts` writes this entry to `.art`.

`art/session/index.html` and `art/session/session-harness.tsx` form a separate lifecycle harness. It mounts `Game` beside an unmount button. `vite.session.config.ts` writes it to `.session`. The harness exists so the browser suite can measure cleanup rather than infer it from a page navigation.

The production build writes `dist/index.html`. Local dependencies live under `node_modules`; browser downloads, temporary browser files, npm cache and test work have separate ignored directories. `test-results` holds browser runtime and journey artifacts. These directories have operational roles but are not additional application source layers.

There is no generated route tree, backend, API client, asset service or utility framework to discover beyond this map. For command ordering see [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md); for import and runtime separation see [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md).

# Shared-device competition$
$
This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.$
$
Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.$
$
## Where the product stands$
$
The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.$
$
This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.$
$
The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.$
$
## Why share a device$
$
A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.$
$
Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.$
$
Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.$
$
## Three things people are following$
$
An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.$
# Competition deals$
$
This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.$
$
The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.$
$
## Deal identity within an event$
$
A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.$
$
For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.$
$
The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.$
$
## The format already implemented$
$
`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.$
$

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.
