# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component or native dialog element. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly. Leave tournament returns to solo play immediately and discards the unfinished bracket state.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game, Tournament and Restart as native buttons. New Game and Restart callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. Tournament preserves the solo game while showing its separate screen. None of these actions consults `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before proceeding.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
# Interface review checklist

This page is a review route through the existing controls, input behavior and related interface policies.

A useful review follows a few populated journeys and checks source at the transitions. An empty board screenshot cannot show preserved drafts, matched-card focus or a stale timer after Restart. The checks below are grounded in the current source and specifications; links identify the separate policies for feature surfaces that do not exist yet.

## Establish what changed

Start with the actual component and its callback. A control can retain its appearance while changing submission, focus or session behavior. A CSS-only change can also alter the hit area or clipping without touching an event handler.

- Identify whether the change affects `Controls`, `Reproduction`, `BoardCodeForm`, `GameStatus`, `Board`, `Card` or the focus hook.
- Follow callbacks into `use-game.ts` and `session.ts` when the change replaces a game, accepts input or publishes feedback.
- Compare element types, ids, label associations, explicit button types and source order as well as class names.
- Check mobile selectors that depend on direct children before accepting a wrapper-only refactor as behaviorally neutral.

The page includes Tournament setup and bracket tables alongside the solo game. Review those surfaces against their own name-entry, table, focus and persistence policies rather than treating them as styling for an existing solo control.

## Deal controls

Use [Control bar](control-bar.md) and the Controls specification as the reference for these observations.

- Grid size is a labeled native select with the seven supported choices, and its selected value agrees with the current game after either successful load type.
- New Game keeps the current size and creates a fresh deal; Restart repeats the current board code.
- Both actions reset selection, pairs, moves and elapsed time, and leave their action button focused.
- Replacing a game during a mismatch does not let an old timer change the replacement.
- The board's next native entry starts at its first card after a replacement, rather than retaining an index from the old deal.

A code comparison can distinguish New Game from Restart even when the two visible decks happen to share some positions. A move-count comparison alone cannot establish that distinction. For size changes, check both card count and the controlled select value.

The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records that separate feature boundary.

## Tournament

Use the Tournament section in [Acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) and the [Competition requirements](../competition/competition-overview.md) to review the one-device knockout.

- The Players select shows 4 or 8 labeled player inputs, and Start tournament enforces normalized names, the 2-to-20 code-point range and distinct names.
- The bracket displays each match's board code, both move/time results and its winner in a captioned table with column headers.
- Both players use the same deal. Start turn, Next turn and Next match appear at the corresponding phase boundaries.
- Export and Load handle setup, active and finished JSON; invalid input preserves the current event.
- Completed events appear in Past tournaments after reload. Leaving early returns to solo play without updating best moves or game size.

## Text tools and errors

The useful draft is one that differs from the currently displayed code, and the useful game state has some progress. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provide the source trace.

- The native disclosure starts collapsed and is named Reproduce a game.
- Board code and Snapshot JSON retain visible, correctly associated labels and their existing native limits.
- Editing Board code, then playing a card, keeps the edited draft.
- Invalid board-code and snapshot submissions preserve the current game and the entered text, and show their exact existing load outcomes.
- Successful Board code submission refreshes the field from the accepted code and updates the selected size.
- Export fills selectable, readable JSON without replacing or pausing play.

Try Enter from Board code as well as clicking Load board. Success focuses Load board because the input is replaced. Failure from the input keeps editing focus there. A click-origin failure keeps focus on the clicked action. The distinction can be lost in a test that only inspects the final board.

The snapshot textarea is multiline and has its own local state. Enter is not an implicit import action. Its draft is not automatically rewritten on every turn or deal replacement. The visible notice sits outside the disclosure, so closing it does not hide an unfinished import's way to continue.

## Import and Resume

A valid unfinished snapshot and a valid completed snapshot exercise different paths. The current specification gives concrete examples and constraints in [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md).

- Unfinished progress loads paused, including an imported position that has not started its clock yet.
- Card activation is blocked while paused, but focus movement still works.
- Resume focuses the board's remembered card before its own button is removed.
- A pending mismatch continues its remaining active interval after Resume.
- Completed progress loads completed, with static completion output and no Resume button.
- Import is not treated as a newly achieved play completion for best-record updates.

A far remembered card on a large board makes the Resume check meaningful. Scroll the board away from that card before resuming and inspect both focus and nearest visibility. Merely finding any focused button afterward would not establish that the remembered destination survived.

## Board movement and activation

Use [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md), [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) and [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) together.

- Tab enters the remembered card and can leave the board again; reverse traversal is native too.
- Plain arrows move one row or column, stop at edges and do not reveal cards.
- Modifier combinations and unlisted keys retain browser behavior.
- Enter, Space, primary click and completed tap reach the shared card action.
- Hover, touch scrolling, pointer cancellation and context-menu interaction do not choose a card.
- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.
- Repeated activation of the first revealed card does not add a move.

For a mismatch, attempt a third activation while the pair is visible and move focus elsewhere. The pair stays until its active wait expires; closure does not drag focus back. Hide and show the page during the interval when a lifecycle change is in scope.

Pointer checks include a card partly clipped at the viewport edge. The source intentionally avoids moving a card under a held pointer, then scrolls it after the click. A centered-card click can pass even when that edge behavior regresses.

## Names and accessible content

Inspect actual DOM and browser accessibility exposure. Visual equivalence is insufficient when hidden data or labels are involved.

- Hidden card names expose position and closed state without a face description or hidden face artwork in their DOM.
- Revealed and matched card names include the correct face description and state.
- Face and check SVGs do not introduce extra focus targets or duplicate the button's description.
- Current statistics expose their visible terms and values without alternate labels replacing the numbers.
- Completion makes the final moves and elapsed time available in the persistent summary.

[Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) records the full journey and the distinction between tree evidence and spoken review. The repository README records the browser and tool versions and says no screen reader was run. A review report should describe the evidence it actually has.

When a feature introduces name input, consult [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The existing code and JSON text fields do not establish those name checks. For new result content, consult [Tables policy](tables-policy.md).

## Results and repeated events

[Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) owns the publication model. In a populated game, inspect the event output while also checking that ordinary rendering stays quiet.

- A first reveal changes the card without publishing a resolved-turn result.
- A match or miss publishes its result once per resolved turn, including consecutive identical misses.
- Focus movement, clock updates and mismatch closure do not repeat the prior result.
- The winning result combines the last match and completion information.
- Repeated invalid loads and repeated successful snapshot loads each publish their load outcome.

The session's `announcement` value and the keyed feedback span explain repeated identical text. A refactor that only compares feedback strings can accidentally remove the event distinction. A refactor that updates the identity on every render can produce the opposite failure.

## Layout and reachability

Read [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md), [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for their detailed scope.

The current visual contract includes a default board fitting a phone, large-board overflow confined to the board viewport and complete focus outlines when cards are brought into view. Review the first, last and an interior card. Container padding can protect corners while an interior nearest-scroll target still clips its outline.

The stated large-board views include `360x800` and `1280x800`. The equivalent zoom layout is `640x400` with device scale 2. Controls, statistics and the completion sentence remain readable in those constrained layouts, with the outer page staying within its viewport width.

Check the expanded reproduction panel as well as the collapsed game. Fields shrink within their rows, action rows wrap and the textarea remains selectable. The native select popup and summary behavior are browser interactions; the surrounding CSS should not be assessed as though they were custom drawn widgets.

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

Tournament mode is a local, shared-device knockout for four or eight entrants. `src/game/Game.tsx` switches between solo play and the Tournament screen. `src/game/tournament` owns entrant setup, bracket rules, turn state, result comparison, JSON exchange and the finished-event history. Tournament play reuses the card rules while keeping its clock and results outside the solo preference session.

This distinction matters during review. Reusing the board is useful only when participant progress, handoffs, scoring and completion remain in the tournament context. The linked pages describe the opening arrangement, event stages, board sizes, deal identity, result comparison and separation from ordinary records.

The solo specification remains version 2.2. Tournament-specific behavior is documented by the Competition pages, including the versioned export and local history in [Tournament JSON](tournament-json.md).

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.
# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The solo game core has no participant collection; Tournament mode keeps entrants and bracket state outside the solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| -------------- | ------- | ---- |
| First          | Ada     | 1    |
| Second         | Bo      | 2    |
| Third          | Cora    | 3    |
| Fourth         | Dev     | 4    |
| Fifth          | Emi     | 5    |
| Sixth          | Finn    | 6    |
| Seventh        | Gia     | 7    |
| Eighth         | Hal     | 8    |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

[Competition deals](competition-deals.md) covers board identity. [Competition ties](competition-ties.md) covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.
# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in [competition pairing](competition-pairing.md), and the dimensions of the playing board are in [competition boards](competition-boards.md).

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.

In the solo branch, `src/game/Game.tsx` passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Tournament mode renders its round label beside the separate tournament controller; neither the solo status component nor session generation represents event progress. [Status bar](../interface/status-bar.md) explains the ordinary statistics, and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains the surrounding composition.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Tournament mode supplies the round text without changing the underlying game mechanics. Reusing the ordinary status component alone still does not supply a round label; the event concept and its rendered location remain separate.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [new game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md) describe the existing interactions.
# Competition results and local records

This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs.

The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.

## The competition boundary

A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.

For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.

The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time.

## What the game saves today

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.

An example stored value is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 10,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 24
  }
}
```

There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.

The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.

[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. Tournament completion does not add fields to this saved preference value. Finished brackets use a separate `neon-pairs.tournaments.v1` local-storage key and a versioned Tournament JSON format described in [Tournament JSON](tournament-json.md). The history keeps the newest ten completed tournaments.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the solo context. Tournament mode avoids both write paths: it keeps the solo session mounted but pauses its clock, and plays in an independent controller rather than calling `replaceGame` or `activateSession`. Consequently neither a tournament board size nor a tournament result changes the solo preference values.

Ordinary session functions do not need a competition argument: tournament play stays outside those functions and holds its state in the tournament controller.

## Where saving actually happens

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.

The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.

`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) cover those existing responsibilities.

## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy

The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.

That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.

`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.

## A concrete review example

Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.

The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.

A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.

The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.

A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:52:The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:58:The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:60:These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:3:This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:5:A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:33:## Active time in the current game
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:35:`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:51:Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:55:The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:65:`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:75:A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.
docs/competition/competition-ties.md:77:For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:32:There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:36:[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. Tournament completion does not add fields to this saved preference value. Finished brackets use a separate `neon-pairs.tournaments.v1` local-storage key and a versioned Tournament JSON format described in [Tournament JSON](tournament-json.md). The history keeps the newest ten completed tournaments.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:40:The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:52:Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:54:The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:60:The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:64:`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:72:A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:19:Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:21:Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:25:An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:27:These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:33:The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:39:## How the current code helps
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:45:The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:5:The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:11:Three settings were considered: a laptop on a table, a tablet passed between adjacent seats and a phone held by the current player. These are contrasting situations, not a representative sample of device usage. Their value was in making different problems observable. A laptop makes spectating easy; a held phone makes physical transfer and changing viewing angles much more prominent.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:13:The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:23:The useful follow-up question was which feature they had noticed, rather than whether they had memorized the official face name. [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) and [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) provide the source context for interpreting such reports.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:31:Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:43:The presentation of a competition handoff remained undecided. The prototype used ordinary play and a paper event sketch. It showed what people looked at and discussed. [Competition overview](competition-overview.md) explains the intended social context.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:59:## Spectators remembered more than the current player expected
docs/competition/competition-research.md:63:This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.
docs/competition/competition-research.md:65:A future research session could explore how different groups feel about spectating, but that is a research question rather than a committed feature. The existing observations support only the narrower conclusion that sharing a device also shares attention in ways that vary with posture, distance and familiarity.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:5:The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:13:The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:21:The exact grammar is in [board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md); the fixed generation algorithm is in [deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md). Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:23:The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:29:The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:33:`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:47:The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:51:A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:55:[Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) explains the ordinary tools, and [competition research](competition-research.md) explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.
